                      MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND
                          ANSWER OF THE APPLICANTS
              TO COMMENTS OF THE PJM MARKET MONITOR AND OF
             PUBLIC CITIZEN, PUBLIC EQUITY STAKEHOLDER PROJECT,
                  AND CITIZENS ACTION COALITION OF INDIANA
                 AND REQUEST FOR CONFIDENTIAL TREATMENT

        On May 21, 2026, Horizon Merger Sub, Inc. (“Horizon Merger Sub”) and The AES

Corporation (“AES”) on behalf of each of its subsidiaries that is or will be a public utility (the

“AES Public Utilities” or “AES Applicants,” and the AES Applicants together with Horizon

Merger Sub, the “Applicants”), submitted an application (“Application”) 1 pursuant to Sections

203(a)(1) and 203(a)(2) of the Federal Power Act, as amended (“FPA”), 2 and Part 33 of the

regulations of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or the “Commission”), 3

requesting authorization for a transaction in which Horizon Merger Sub will merge with and into

AES, with AES continuing as the surviving corporation (“Transaction”). Upon consummation of

the Transaction, AES will be jointly owned: (i) 36.625 percent by investment funds and vehicles

controlled or managed by affiliates of Global Infrastructure Management, LLC (together with such

affiliates, “GIP”), a consolidated subsidiary of BlackRock, Inc. (“BlackRock”), (ii) 33.375 percent

    Power Act, and Requests for Limited Waivers and Confidential Treatment, Docket No. EC26-99-000 (filed May

 by investment funds, vehicles, and/or separate accounts managed and/or advised by controlled

affiliates of EQT AB (together, with such affiliates “EQT AB”); (iii) 10 percent by investment

funds and vehicles controlled or managed by Qatar Investment Authority (“QIA”), and (iv) 20

percent by investment funds and vehicles owned by California Public Employees’ Retirement

System (“CalPERS”), under a passive ownership structure in which CalPERS’ interests will be

controlled or managed by GIP. 4 Accordingly, upon close of the Transaction, investment funds or

vehicles of the following entities are expected to directly own AES: GIP, EQT, and QIA as non-

passive owners and CalPERS as a passive owner (collectively, the “Purchasers”). GIP and EQT

will have co-governance rights in AES.

        On July 20, 2026, Public Citizen, Private Equity Stakeholder Project, and Citizens Action

Coalition of Indiana (collectively, the “Joint Protestors”) filed a joint protest of the Transaction. 5

The Independent Market Monitor (“IMM” and together with the Joint Protestors, the “Protestors”)

for PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) also filed comments alleging that the Application was

deficient and that any authorization of the Transaction should include a series of behavioral

commitments. 6

        The Protestors expend little effort arguing that the Transaction does not satisfy the

Commission’s well-established test for authorization under Section 203 because it easily does so.

The Protestors instead engage in collateral attacks on orders not at issue in this proceeding,

forth by the Protestors would deter investment in American energy companies, at the expense of

everyday Americans, at a time when energy affordability and reliability are imperative and

investment in the electric industry is paramount to the future economy. The Commission should

reject the arguments raised by the Protestors and authorize the Transaction without further delay.

I.        MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER

          Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of FERC’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, 7 Applicants

hereby move for leave to submit this answer (“Answer”) in response to the Joint Protest and IMM

Comments. As discussed herein, the Joint Protest and IMM Comments contain irrelevant,

meritless, and unsupported arguments regarding the Applicants and the Application. This Answer

addresses those arguments and clarifies the record. The Commission regularly accepts otherwise

impermissible answers where, as here, an answer promotes the Commission’s understanding of

the issues raised in the proceeding. 8 Good cause exists to accept this Answer because it corrects

misstatements of fact and will help the Commission make a reasoned decision with respect to the

Application.

II.       ANSWER

          A.       The Commission should reject arguments regarding BlackRock’s Blanket
                   Authorization as outside the scope of this proceeding and not relevant to its
                   review of the Transaction.

          The Joint Protest essentially asks the Commission to reevaluate its 2025 decision granting

BlackRock its existing Blanket Authorization. Such a request is outside the scope of this

         On April 17, 2025, the Commission extended BlackRock’s blanket authorization under

FPA Section 203(a)(2) to acquire voting securities of any “public utility,” “electric utility

company,” “transmitting utility,” or “holding company in a holding company system that includes

an electric utility company or transmitting utility” for an additional three years, subject to certain

conditions (“Blanket Authorization”). 9               The conditions placed on BlackRock’s Blanket

Authorization include, among other things, that BlackRock’s managed funds and investment

accounts may not collectively own or control more than 20 percent, and no fund or investment

account may individually own more than 10 percent, of the voting securities of any one U.S.

Traded Utility, and that BlackRock “may not exercise day-to-day management or operations of

any U.S. Trading Utility whose voting securities are acquired pursuant to the Blanket

Authorizations, except pursuant to separate authorizations under [S]ection 203 of the FPA.”10 In

reauthorizing and extending BlackRock’s Blanket Authorization, the Commission explained that:

                  adversely impact competition in any market. Additionally, the

The Commission also addressed arguments raised by Public Citizen and the Private Equity

Stakeholder Project that BlackRock’s non-controlling investment management operations under

its Blanket Authorization and its active ownership interests in public utilities such as ALLETE

create a conflict of interest and is a violation of the terms of its Blanket Authorization. 12 There,

the Commission held that BlackRock’s investment activity and request for reauthorization “is

consistent with [its] prior orders allowing BlackRock and others under the blanket authorization

upon receiving separate approval under FPA [S]ection 203.” 13 In fact, the Commission explained,

BlackRock has “had concurrent holdings of both controlling and non-controlling interests in

different public utilities since the grant of their original Blanket Authorization[] without

invalidating the terms of the Blank Authorization[].” 14 The arguments raised by the Protestors

with respect to any alleged conflict of interest between this Transaction and BlackRock’s holdings

under its Blanket Authorization are misplaced and have been previously rejected by the

Commission. The Commission should reject them again here.

         Specifically, there is not and cannot be a conflict with or any violation of BlackRock’s

Blanket Authorization as a result of GIP’s proposed acquisition of non-passive interests in the AES

Public Utilities and its non-controlling, passive holdings under its Blanket Authorization as alleged

by the IMM. 15 To the contrary, the Blanket Authorization expressly requires BlackRock to get

           Nor could there be any nefarious coordination and use of non-public information by

BlackRock with respect to U.S. Traded Utilities under its Blanket Authorization and public utilities

in which it owns active interests. 16 First, contrary to the IMM’s assertion, a minority position in a

public company’s common stock does not provide shareholders with a right to “access to

the Blanket Authorization conditions remain “sufficient to ensure that [BlackRock is] not able to

influence or exert control over the public utilities” in which it holds interests under its Blanket

Authorization. 18 Third, as noted above, the Blanket Authorization expressly permits BlackRock

authorized pursuant to a separate Section 203 proceeding. 19 The IMM also questions whether this

Transaction should result in BlackRock’s passive investments continuing to be treated as passive. 20

This argument is a red herring. The proposed Transaction has no impact on, nor does it change,

any other BlackRock investments, including its passive investments in AES—which will be taken

         B.       The Application properly provided all requisite data for the Commission to
                  find that the Transaction is consistent with the public interest and that the
                  Transaction will not result in any adverse effect on competition.

         The IMM erroneously accuses the Applicants of failing to identify and consider “qualifying

facilities” (“QFs”) or behind the meter facilities in its market power analysis. 22 The Applicants’

QF data was provided as part of the affidavit of Ms. Julie Solomon and Dr. Jeffrey Opgrand

(“Secretariat Affidavit”), including Exhibits SEC-3a, SEC-3b, SEC-3c, SEC-4a, and SEC-5a.23

With respect to QFs under 1 MW, the Application explained that such generators are too small to

participate in Regional Transmission Organization or Independent System Operator markets

unless aggregated. Although aggregated distributed energy resource (“DER”) aggregations (“DER

Aggregations”) were permitted to participate in the base residual auction as of the 2028/2029

Delivery Year, zero DER offers were submitted in the 2028/2029 Delivery Year base residual

auction. 24 Further, DER Aggregations will not be able to participate in PJM’s energy and ancillary

services markets until February 1, 2028. 25 Accordingly, the IMM’s request to supplement the

Application with QFs under 1 MW that “would participate as part of a DER Aggregation

Resources in PJM” is misplaced. 26

           The Applicants conservatively included a delivered price test (“DPT”) for PJM and its

relevant submarkets, 27 despite the fact that the installed capacity analysis demonstrated that the

Transaction would result in a combined affiliated generation portfolio of 2.6% of PJM’s installed

capacity, clearly within the range the Commission has deemed to be de minimis. Further, the DPT

determined that the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (“HHI”) changes were 13 points or less in an

unconcentrated PJM market under all scenarios. 28 The generation overlap in PJM is arguably de

minimis and does not present any horizontal market power concerns. Any possible aggregation of

DERs could not have a material impact on this analysis until a meaningful amount of DER

Aggregations participate in PJM’s energy and capacity markets, given that—as the IMM

acknowledges—DER Aggregations cannot currently participate in PJM’s energy and ancillary

services markets. 29

                   1.      Implementation of the IMM’s alternative market power analysis is
                          unjustified.

          The IMM acknowledges that the Transaction “does not fail the Commission’s HHI

thresholds in the Applicants’ [DPT]” and that “[t]he Commission does not require a pivotal

supplier analysis in the initial evidentiary support in applications for approval of transactions that

pass the Commission’s market power screens, based on the DPT.” 39 The IMM nevertheless pushes

forward with an alternative analysis based on its opinion that the DPT analysis “does not ensure

that the Transaction does not increase market power.” 40 It does so by analyzing constraints that

are binding more than 876 hours or 5% of hours during April 2024 through March 2026. 41 As the

Commission has previously explained, the identification of binding constraints alone is not

sufficient to demonstrate a submarket nor does that data “explain how the constraints are

distinguishable from existing submarkets in PJM.” 42 The Commission has recently rejected the

application of the IMM’s alternative analysis accordingly, explaining that:

                  With respect to the PJM IMM’s alternative analyses for the
                  aggregate PJM energy market, proposed local energy markets, and
                  the PJM capacity market, including its reliance on the three pivotal
                  supplier test, the Commission has previously explained that it
                  historically has not relied on three pivotal supplier test results for
                  analysis of FPA section 203 transactions and that three pivotal
                  supplier analyses are not required from applicants seeking
                  authorization for a proposed transaction under FPA section 203.
                  Consistent with this precedent, we will not rely on the PJM IMM’s
                  three pivotal supplier test results or analysis in this proceeding.

          The Commission’s rationale for rejecting the IMM’s alternative analysis and adhering to

the DPT analysis is well-established. The DPT is “intended to identify mergers that clearly do not

raise competitive concerns early in the process and . . . produces a reliable, generally conservative

analysis of the competitive effects of a proposed merger.” 44 The point of the test is to identify

transactions that “clearly do not raise competitive concerns.” 45 Such is the case here. The DPT

analysis performed with respect to the Transaction demonstrates that the Transaction will not result

in a single screen violation during any season and under any price sensitivity. 46

                       2.        The IMM’s request to restrict removal of generation assets is misplaced.
